Categorical Omega for Ordered-Categorical Items, With a Confidence Interval

Source: R/reliability_omega_categorical.R
reliability_omega_categorical.Rd

Estimates categorical omega (\(\omega_C\); Green & Yang, 2009; Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016) for a homogeneous composite of ordered-categorical items and returns a bootstrap confidence interval. The denominator argument selects whether the variance of the summed categories is built from the unrestricted polychoric correlations ("observed", the default) or from the polychoric correlations the fitted single-factor model reproduces ("model_implied", the coefficient as Green and Yang, 2009, defined it). Incomplete rows are set aside by listwise deletion (the default) or used through pairwise deletion or multiple imputation (missing); under multiple imputation the interval is formed by bootstrap then impute (Schomaker & Heumann, 2018).

Usage

reliability_omega_categorical(
  data,
  ci_method = c("bca", "percentile", "bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic", "none"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  B = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  denominator = c("observed", "model_implied"),
  ncpus = 1L,
  missing = c("listwise", "pairwise", "mi"),
  aux = NULL,
  impute = c("pmm", "polr"),
  imputations = 20L,
  progress = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A numeric matrix or data frame of three or more ordered-categorical items (integer codes for the categories), plus any auxiliary variables named in aux. Only the order of an item's codes matters: its categories are scored 0, 1, ..., \(C - 1\) (see How the categories are scored in Details). A factor whose labels are whole numbers is read as those numbers, so a factor labeled 0 to 4 is the item coded 0 to 4, under every treatment of missing; a factor whose labels are words is refused, as is an ordered factor whose levels are not in the order of the numbers they name. A column read with haven is read as its values, with SPSS user-defined missing values made missing. Incomplete rows are treated as missing says; under the default they are set aside. With two items the single-factor model is not identified (their one polychoric correlation determines only the product of the two loadings), and the function stops.

ci_method

Method for constructing the confidence interval. See Details. When not supplied, no interval is computed: every interval for categorical omega is bootstrap based, and a bootstrap is never run unless requested. Ask for "bca" (the recommended method) or "percentile" to obtain one.

conf_level

Confidence level for the interval. Defaults to 0.95.

B

Number of bootstrap replications. The default, NULL, is 10000 under missing = "listwise" and "pairwise", where BCa, the recommended interval, reads its limits from extreme quantiles, and 1000 under missing = "mi", where each replication is imputed imputations times and refitted on each, and the percentile interval is the recommended one (see Run time under multiple imputation). When no item value is missing, missing = "mi" has nothing to impute and returns the complete data result, whose bootstrap refits once per replication, so the default there is 10000, as the message says. When a bootstrap is requested, B (supplied or default) must be a single whole number of at least the count the interval method and the level require, as in the rest of the family: at the default conf_level, 400 for "percentile" (10 replications beyond each limit), 2000 for "bca" (50 beyond each nominal limit), and 100 for the two bootstrap standard error methods; at 0.99 the first two are 2000 and 10000, so the default of 1000 under missing = "mi" does not serve a 99 percent percentile interval and the refusal names the number. A smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). When fewer replications than required return a value the interval is withheld under a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. See dmar_bootstrap, which also describes options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) for a first look with a smaller B.

seed

Random number seed used for bootstrap reproducibility. Defaults to NULL, under which the resamples are drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream; supply an integer for a reproducible interval, which is set for the call only, the caller's random number state being restored when it returns.

denominator

How the polychoric correlations behind the total variance in the denominator are estimated: "observed" (the default; the unrestricted polychoric correlations) or "model_implied" (the correlations reproduced by the fitted single-factor model, as in Green and Yang, 2009). See Details. Every interval method applies to both settings, since every interval here is bootstrap based and each replication recomputes the coefficient with the same denominator.

ncpus

The number of processes over which the bootstrap replications are spread. The default 1 runs them in this R session; a larger number uses forked workers (boot's parallel = "multicore") or, on Windows, which cannot fork, a socket cluster ("snow"), whose workers load the installed DMAR. boot draws every resample before any replication runs, so a given seed returns the same interval, counts, and replicates whatever ncpus is. A session that forks workers and also starts background processes through callr or processx needs the environment variable PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD set before processx is loaded (see sem_exact_fit_bootstrap). Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

missing

How incomplete rows of data are treated: "listwise" (the default; only complete rows are analyzed), "pairwise" (each threshold and polychoric correlation from the rows that observe its items), or "mi" (multiple imputation, with a bootstrap then impute interval). Listwise and pairwise deletion are consistent only when values are missing completely at random; multiple imputation when they are missing at random given the items and aux. See Missing data in Details.

aux

Optional character vector naming columns of data that are auxiliary variables: numeric predictors in the imputation model, never items, so they inform the imputations without entering the composite (the inclusive strategy of Collins, Schafer, & Kam, 2001). Supplying aux implies missing = "mi", as it implies full information maximum likelihood in reliability_omega; with "listwise" or "pairwise" named explicitly it is an error.

impute

The imputation model under missing = "mi": "pmm" (the default; predictive mean matching) or "polr" (the proportional odds model). See The imputation model in Details. Supplying it with another missing is an error.

imputations

Under missing = "mi", the number of imputations of each bootstrap replication (at least 2, default 20), which is also the least number of imputations behind the point estimate (whose number is at least 20 and may be raised by von Hippel's rule; see The number of imputations). Supplying it with another missing is an error.

progress

NULL (the default), or a function of two arguments that the bootstrap calls as it runs, so that an application can show how far a long bootstrap has gone and let its user stop it (a Shiny app, for example). It is called as progress(done, total), with the number of replications attempted so far and B: after each replication when ncpus = 1, and with more processes after each block of replications they complete together, about a fiftieth of B (ncpus * ceiling(B / (50 * ncpus)) replications, the last block possibly fewer), so that done advances by the block. A BCa interval takes its acceleration from a regression on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications return a value as there are cases, and from the jackknife, one leave-one-out refit per case, when fewer do or when that regression fails or gives influence values that are not all finite; the jackknife runs at most once in a call, and not at all when no interval is formed or every returned replicate has the same value. While it runs, the callback is called again after each refit (with more processes, after each block of ncpus * ceiling(n / (50 * ncpus)) refits, n the number of cases resampled), with done and total both B, so it can be called more than B times, and done equal to total does not mean that the bootstrap has finished. If the callback returns FALSE, the bootstrap stops before the next replication or block with an error of class dmar_bootstrap_cancelled, whose elements done and total say how far it got (see dmar_metadata); any other value is ignored. An error inside the callback stops the call with an error of class dmar_progress_error, whose message names the callback and which carries done, total, and, as parent, the callback's own condition with its class intact, so that an application can tell a failing callback from a failing analysis. The callback runs outside the random number stream, so a given seed returns the same result with or without it, and a callback that draws random numbers leaves the caller's stream as it found it. With NULL nothing is called. Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value and rows "estimate" (sample \(\omega_C\)), "se" (the bootstrap standard deviation across replications, already on the coefficient scale; NA for ci_method = "none"), "ci_lower" and "ci_upper" (clamped to [0, 1]), "conf_level", "N" (the rows analyzed: the complete rows under listwise deletion, otherwise the rows with at least one observed item, and under multiple imputation with aux also the rows with an observed auxiliary variable), "N_complete" (the rows complete on the items; equal to "N" under listwise deletion, and carried so the whole reliability family returns one shape), and "n_items" (number of items); the rows are the same under every missing. Under missing = "mi" the estimate is the mean over the imputations of the observed data and se is the standard error of that mean from the bootstrap (see The number of imputations). Attributes coefficient ("omega_categorical"), denominator ("observed" or "model_implied"), missing ("listwise", "pairwise", or "mi"; "listwise" also when the items are complete and another treatment had nothing to do), aux (when supplied), ci_method (under missing = "mi" the method followed by "(bootstrap then impute)"), and B record the computation. The attribute residual_cor carries the local dependence summary of the single-factor fit: a list with matrix (the unrestricted polychoric correlations minus those the model reproduces, named by item), largest (the residual correlation largest in absolute value, with its sign), items (the pair it belongs to), and saturated; a pair whose polychoric correlation the data do not determine has an NA residual and is passed over. With three items the single-factor model is saturated (zero degrees of freedom) and reproduces every polychoric correlation, so its residuals are zero and carry no information about local dependence: saturated is then TRUE, largest is NA, and items is NULL, rather than naming whichever pair carries the largest rounding error. The printed table names the denominator and the largest residual correlation (or says that the model is saturated) in two lines under the table. A bootstrap call also carries the attribute bootstrap, a list recording the replications the interval conditions on: attempted (B), returned (the replications whose value the interval uses; the standard error is their standard deviation and the percentile and BCa limits are their quantiles), failed (the difference), reasons (a named count of why replications were set aside: error when the refit raised an error, non_finite when it was set aside without one, as a fit that lavaan stopped or that did not converge is, as an improper one is, and, under the observed denominator, as one that left a polychoric correlation undetermined is, and, under either, as one whose determined correlations leave the loadings unidentified is), error_messages (the distinct error messages with their counts, empty when none), undetermined (the replications set aside because the resample left a polychoric correlation undetermined, which the observed setting needs, or left correlations undetermined whose absence leaves the loadings unidentified, under either setting; see Details), improper (the replications set aside because their single-factor solution was improper, with a standardized loading above one, which is an error variance below zero), improper_kept (always zero here: categorical omega is not defined for an improper solution, so such a replication has no estimate to keep), improper_rule ("drop", for the same reason), no_solution (always zero here: it counts the replications that reliability_omega sets aside because the correlations of three items admit no single-factor solution, a check the categorical fit does not make), not_converged (zero here: a fit that did not converge is counted among the non_finite ones), too_few_cases (always zero here: it counts the replications that reliability_omega sets aside for too few distinct cases, a rule the categorical fit does not apply), caution (TRUE when the replications set aside number at least \((1 - C)/2\) of B, with \(C\) the confidence level, so that where they would have fallen can decide a limit), require_half (TRUE: no interval is formed when fewer than half of the replications return a value), required, bootstrap_status, and B_used (the fewest replications a request may ask for, the verdict of the rule, and the count the limits rest on, as in reliability_alpha), acceleration and acceleration_method (the BCa acceleration used and whether it came from the regression or the jackknife; NA unless a BCa interval was formed), jackknife (the same attempted, returned, failed, reasons, error_messages, undetermined, improper, improper_kept, no_solution, not_converged, and too_few_cases for the leave-one-out refits behind the acceleration, all zero when no jackknife ran), ncpus (the number of processes used), t (the estimate of every replication, in order, NA where there is none), and status (a factor giving the fate of every replication, with levels "proper", "improper", "error", "non_finite", "undetermined", and "not_converged"; the interval uses those whose status is "proper"). The attribute B_used is the number of replications the interval uses (returned; when fewer than half returned a value, or fewer than required, no interval is formed). The attributes n_dropped, B_required, and bootstrap_status repeat the counts in the names every bootstrap result of the package carries (see dmar_bootstrap). The printed table shows these counts in one line, and a warning states them whenever a replication was set aside or the caution applies.

Under missing = "mi" the bootstrap attribute has the same elements, with three differences: reasons has a third count, imputation, for the replications whose imputation itself failed (not part of non_finite), whose messages are in imputation_messages; status has a seventh level, "imputation"; and a replication counted under another reason is one in which fewer than half of its completed data sets returned a value, the first that returned none deciding the reason. The jackknife counts are zero, since BCa is refused. The attribute imputation is a list: impute; imputations_point (\(M_0\), the imputations of the observed data behind the point estimate); imputations_returned (those of them that returned a value, which the estimate averages); imputations_set_aside (the others, counted by reason: improper, undetermined, error, non_converged, and non_finite); imputations_replicate (imputations); imputations_floor (max(imputations, 20)); imputations_rule (the number von Hippel's rule asks for); maxit (10, the iterations of the chained equations); estimates (the \(M_0\) completed data estimates, NA where one was set aside), status (the fate of each: "proper" or the reason it was set aside), and between_sd (the standard deviation of those that returned a value); sd_replicates (the standard deviation of the replicate means); s2_boot, s2_imp, fmi, and fmi_ci_upper (the sampling and imputation variances, the fraction of missing information, and its 95% upper limit); widening (\(\sqrt{1 + \gamma / M_b}\), the factor by which imputation noise widens the percentile interval); replicate_estimates (the B by imputations matrix of completed data estimates, NA where one returned no value; NULL without a bootstrap); replicate_sets_set_aside (the completed data sets set aside within the replications that returned a value, counted by the reasons of imputations_set_aside; NULL without a bootstrap); polr_fallbacks (how often the proportional odds model fell back to a multinomial model, in the point estimate's imputations and in the replications); ridge (how often mice applied its ridge penalty, counted the same way); and aux_set_aside (the auxiliary variables left out of the imputation model as linear functions of other predictors, character(0) when none). The components that need the bootstrap are NA without one. Under missing = "pairwise" or "mi" the printed table adds a line naming the treatment and its assumption, and under "mi" a line giving the number of imputations, the fraction of missing information, and the widening (none when no interval is reported).

Details

Categorical omega is designed for items measured on an ordered categorical scale (e.g., Likert items). It uses a probit-link single-factor model in which each observed item \(X_j\) is modeled as a categorization of an underlying continuous response variable \(X_j^{*}\) via thresholds \(t_{j,c}\) (Muthén, 1984; Millsap & Yun-Tein, 2004), fit by diagonally weighted least squares with mean- and variance-adjusted test statistic (WLSMV), the standard estimator for ordered categorical items. With the delta parameterization (\(Var(X_j^{*}) = 1\)), the population categorical omega is $$\omega_C = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{J} \sum_{j'=1}^{J} \sigma_{jj'}\!\left(\lambda_{j}\lambda_{j'}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{J} \sum_{j'=1}^{J} \sigma_{jj'}\!\left(\rho_{X_{j}^{*} X_{j'}^{*}}\right)},$$ where \(\sigma_{jj'}(r)\) is the covariance of \((X_{j}, X_{j'})\) computed from a bivariate normal CDF over pairs of category thresholds and a latent-response correlation \(r\) (Green & Yang, 2009, Eq. 13–14, with the full coefficient their Eq. 21; Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016, Eq. 17–18). The numerator uses the correlations of the common part, \(\lambda_j \lambda_{j'}\), under either setting of denominator; the two settings differ in the correlations \(\rho\) used for the total variance. The bivariate normal probabilities, one for each pair of thresholds of each pair of items, are computed by DMAR itself, by the method of Drezner and Wesolowsky (1990) as refined by Genz (2004), which is the algorithm mvtnorm applies in two dimensions. The two agree to within \(4 \times 10^{-16}\), except within about \(10^{-7}\) of a correlation of one, where mvtnorm loses accuracy and DMAR's computation does not. Computed together, the probabilities take a small fraction of the time of the factor model's fit.

"observed" (default)

The unrestricted polychoric correlations, estimated from the data by a saturated bivariate model (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016, Eq. 18). Structure that the single-factor model omits, such as a pair of items with shared wording, stays in the total variance, which makes this the categorical counterpart of robust omega (see reliability_omega). It is the coefficient MBESS::ci.reliability(type = "categorical") computes, apart from the samples described below in which the data do not determine a polychoric correlation.

"model_implied"

The latent-response correlations reproduced by the fitted single-factor model. This is categorical omega as Green and Yang (2009) defined it: their appendix program takes “the reproduced (model-based) correlation matrix” as the input to the denominator, so correlated errors enter the total variance only when they are specified in the model.

When the single-factor model reproduces the polychoric correlations the two settings coincide, and they diverge as the model misfits. Neither protects the numerator: shared structure among a few items raises their loadings under either setting. The result therefore reports the residual polychoric correlations (the unrestricted minus the reproduced) and prints the largest under the table, so that a high coefficient resting on redundant items is visible beside it. When the shared structure sits on the items that dominate the factor, the factor absorbs it and the residuals appear among the other items, so the largest residual signals local dependence more reliably than it locates it.

What each denominator describes. Both settings share the numerator, the variance of the summed categories attributable to the single factor, and differ in what they take the total variance of the sum to be. The model implied setting takes the variance the fitted single-factor model reproduces, so the coefficient describes the sum score as the model describes it: covariance the model omits is absent from the numerator and from the denominator alike. The observed setting takes the variance implied by the polychoric correlations estimated without the single-factor restriction (still under the latent-response model that defines polychoric correlations), so covariance the model omits is counted as variance of the sum that the factor does not explain. The two estimate the same quantity when the model holds. Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) used the observed setting because the total variance of the sum score is a property of the data and need not be taken from a model that may be wrong; Green and Yang (2009) used the model implied setting, which is the reliability of the sum score under the fitted model.

How the categories are scored. Categorical omega is the reliability of a sum in which each item's categories are scored as consecutive ranks, 0, 1, ..., \(C - 1\), in the order of the item's codes: Green and Yang (2009, Eq. 11) and Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016, Eq. 16) define the observed item as \(X_{ij} = c\) for \(c = 0, 1, \ldots, C - 1\), and MBESS and semTools compute the same coefficient. The function therefore uses the order of the codes in data, not their values, and the coefficient is that of the sum of the codes as given whenever every item's codes are equally spaced with one step shared by all the items (codes 0, 2, 4, 6 on every item give the same result as 1, 2, 3, 4). When they are not, as with codes -2, -1, 1, 2, with items stepping by 2 beside items stepping by 1, or with a category between two used ones that no respondent chose, the sum of the codes is a different composite, and a message says so and names the items; the coefficient is still that of the ranks. In the examples behind this paragraph the coded sum's reliability was lower by 0.009 to 0.012 for codes -2, -1, 1, 2 on every item and by 0.034 for two three-category items coded 1, 3, 5 beside two coded 1, 2, 3, and an unused interior category changed it by about 0.001.

When the data do not determine a polychoric correlation. The observed setting needs every unrestricted polychoric correlation. When two items are skewed in opposite directions, as in Green and Yang's (2009) mixed-skew conditions, their bivariate table can have empty cells in a pattern (every respondent below the top category of one item in the bottom category of the other) that leaves the polychoric correlation without a finite standard error. The unrestricted value is then arbitrary, and the single-factor fit gives the correlation no weight, so the loadings rest on the correlations the data do determine. Those identify the loadings only when they connect every item to the others, directly or through other items, and include at least one cycle of an odd number of items, such as three items whose three correlations are all determined (the graph whose edges are the determined pairs must be connected and not bipartite); an item joined to the rest by a single determined correlation is then identified as well. When every correlation between y1 or y2 and y3 or y4 of the example below is undetermined, the determined ones fix only the products of the loadings of y1 and y2 and of y3 and y4: the relative sign of the two pairs is free, and lavaan's default start values can return loadings of opposite signs and a categorical omega near 0.05, where the population value is 0.716. In 60 samples of 300 from that design, 13 had determined correlations that did not identify the loadings: 2 with that sign reversal (0.05 and 0.09), 8 whose value moved with the start values by up to 0.06, and 3 whose default start values gave an improper solution. The function therefore checks the graph. When the determined correlations identify the loadings, the observed setting stops with an error naming the pair and pointing to the model implied setting, and the model implied setting proceeds, says which pair it set aside, and reports that pair's residual correlation as NA. When they do not, both settings stop with an error naming the pairs and the blocks of items no determined correlation joins, since the numerator takes the loadings under either setting. The unrestricted polychoric correlations come from the single-factor fit itself, which agrees with a second, saturated fit whenever every correlation is determined. MBESS computes them from such a saturated fit, which returns 0 for an undetermined correlation and so removes the pair from the total variance without a message. The example below uses Green and Yang's design at a sample size where samples rarely have this problem; at \(N = 500\) most of them do.

A bootstrap meets the problem far more often than the sample does. The few respondents in the sparse cells of an oppositely skewed pair are what determine its polychoric correlation, and a resample omits some of them as a matter of course, so a sample whose correlations are all determined still yields many resamples in which one is not. On the data of the example below, which have no such pair, about half of the replications of a bootstrap of the observed setting have one (80, 95, and 97 of 200 in percentile bootstraps with seed 1, 2, and 3). Those replications are set aside, counted in the bootstrap attribute (undetermined; see Value), named in the printed line and in a warning, and the interval then conditions on the replications that redrew the respondents who determine the correlation, which is not the bootstrap distribution of the coefficient; with more than half set aside, no interval is reported (see below), and on these data the observed setting is always near that point. The model implied setting needs no unrestricted polychoric correlation and sets aside only the replications whose determined correlations leave the loadings unidentified (counted as undetermined as well), so with items skewed in opposite directions it keeps more of them, but how many it keeps depends on the sample size. In a percentile bootstrap of the example's complete data (\(N = 1000\), B = 200, seed = 1) it set aside 1 replication of 200, and over 20 samples of that size from the design (B = 50) none in 15 and at most 18%. Under pairwise deletion of the example's incomplete copy it set aside 47 of 200: 27 whose loadings were unidentified, 3 improper, and 17 whose fit failed, so the caution applies. At \(N = 300\), in the 45 samples of 60 whose point estimate was identified and proper, it set aside a median of 42% of the replications (B = 50): 18% where the sample determined every correlation, 40% where it left one undetermined, and 64% where it left two, and more than half in 15 of the 45. When fewer than half of the replications return a value, no interval is reported (see below). Under either denominator, a replication whose determined correlations do not identify the loadings is set aside rather than evaluated at arbitrary starting values.

When the solution is improper. With few respondents in the extreme categories, or an item that nearly duplicates the factor, the single-factor fit can return a standardized loading above one, a negative residual variance (a Heywood case). Categorical omega is not defined for such a solution, since its assembly evaluates the bivariate normal distribution at the item's communality, and the function stops with an error naming the item and its loading under either setting of denominator. A bootstrap replication with an improper solution is set aside and counted (improper in the bootstrap attribute); these are the replications in which a standardized loading ran past one (an error variance fell below zero), so setting them aside can trim the upper tail of the bootstrap distribution, which is why their number is reported.

Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) found in extensive Monte Carlo simulation that the bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap confidence interval for categorical omega achieved acceptable coverage across a wide variety of threshold patterns, sample sizes, item counts, and population reliability values, with one documented exception: coverage dipped somewhat below the acceptable range when the number of items and the population reliability were both high. They specifically recommend BCa for categorical omega. Because no bootstrap runs in DMAR unless the user requests one, the default output is the point estimate with a message naming the call that produces the recommended interval; request ci_method = "bca" to obtain it. The interval is not a quick one. Every replication refits the ordered-categorical factor model, whose sample statistics also supply the unrestricted polychoric correlations behind the denominator. That is a fraction of a second for a scale of moderate length, so the recommended interval at the default B = 10000 can run for several minutes; when B is below the number of cases, the jackknife behind the BCa acceleration adds one such refit per case (at the default B the acceleration is read from the replicates themselves at no extra cost; see the "bca" entry below). The example on this page therefore stops at the point estimate; the reported analysis adds ci_method = "bca" to the same call, with seed for reproducibility, and for these oppositely skewed items it bootstraps the model implied setting, which at this sample size keeps nearly all of the replications of the complete data (see above), or reports how many replications of the observed setting were set aside.

When to use. Use reliability_omega_categorical when items are ordered-categorical, especially when (a) the number of categories is small (e.g., two to five), (b) item distributions are skewed, or (c) threshold patterns differ markedly across items. In Kelley and Pornprasertmanit's (2016) Study 3, treating ordered items as continuous and using reliability_omega with the observed total variance in the denominator achieved acceptable coverage only when threshold patterns were similar across items; in their experience that condition is rare in practice.

Available confidence interval methods (set via ci_method). Every interval here is bootstrap based: the rows of data are resampled with replacement B times (10000 by default, 1000 under missing = "mi"; see Missing data below) and categorical omega is recomputed, with the full WLSMV model refit, on each replication (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). Replications whose refit fails or does not converge, most common with small samples and sparse response categories, are set aside, as are replications with an improper solution, replications that leave a polychoric correlation undetermined under the observed setting, and replications whose determined correlations leave the loadings unidentified under either setting (all described above), and the interval is computed from the replications that return a value: the standard error is their standard deviation, and the percentile and BCa limits are quantiles of the returned replicates, not of all B. How many were attempted, how many returned a value, and why the rest were set aside is recorded in the bootstrap attribute of the result (see Value), printed in one line under the table, and stated in a warning whenever a replication was set aside, so an interval that conditions on a subset of the replications says so and by how much. When fewer than half of the replications return a value, no interval is reported: the standard error and the limits are NA, and the warning and the printed line say why. The rest would be a minority of the resamples, chosen by whether they returned a value, and their spread would describe those resamples rather than the sampling distribution of the coefficient; this is the criterion by which the point estimate under missing = "mi" stops when fewer than half of its completed data sets return a value (Lim & Cheung, 2022, p. 1069). The remedy is a larger sample, which fills the sparse cells of the bivariate tables. Bootstrap results vary from run to run; supply seed for reproducibility.

"bca"

The bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap, the default and the specific recommendation of Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016). Where the percentile interval reads its limits directly off the empirical quantiles of the bootstrap estimates, BCa adjusts the two quantile positions for median bias (estimated from the bootstrap distribution) and for the rate at which the estimator's variance changes with the parameter (the acceleration, estimated by the jackknife), making it second-order accurate where the percentile interval is first-order accurate (DiCiccio & Efron, 1996). The adjusted quantile positions sit farther into the tails than the percentile interval uses, which is why the default B = 10000 is larger than the customary 2000; reduce B for exploration, not for a reported analysis. The acceleration is estimated as boot estimates it: by regressing the bootstrap replicates on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications as cases returned a value, at no extra cost, and otherwise, or when that regression fails, by the jackknife, one leave-one-out refit per case. A leave-one-out refit that fails (when a case is the only respondent in one of an item's categories, for example) is counted and set aside, and the acceleration is estimated from the refits that returned a value. When the acceleration cannot be estimated at all (fewer than two leave-one-out refits returned a value), or the bias correction cannot be (every returned replicate on one side of the estimate), the percentile interval is returned in its place with a warning, and the ci_method attribute records the substitution as "percentile (BCa acceleration could not be estimated: ...)". The counts of leave-one-out refits and the acceleration used are in the bootstrap attribute.

"percentile"

Percentile bootstrap: the interval limits are the empirical quantiles of the bootstrap estimates.

"bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic"

Wald intervals using the bootstrap standard deviation as a standard error, built on the logit scale for the _logistic variant so the endpoints respect [0, 1]. Under missing = "mi" the standard error is that of the point estimate (see The number of imputations below).

"none"

Return only the point estimate.

Under missing = "mi" the percentile interval is the recommended one and BCa is refused (see Missing data).

Missing data. The missing argument sets how incomplete rows of data are treated. Under "pairwise" and "mi", rows with no observed item, which carry no information about the items, are set aside, as under full information maximum likelihood elsewhere in the family, and when no item value is missing in the rows that remain both return the complete data result, with a message. Under multiple imputation a row with no observed item is kept when an auxiliary variable is observed on it, and its items are imputed from the auxiliaries, as full information maximum likelihood elsewhere in the family keeps such a row: setting it aside would make the analysis conditional on having an observed item, which biases the estimate when the items go missing together at random given the auxiliaries.

"listwise" (default)

Only the rows observed on every column of data are analyzed. Listwise deletion is consistent when values are missing completely at random (MCAR), and even then it discards what the incomplete rows say about the items they observe. When fewer than two rows are complete, or an item takes a single value in the complete rows, the function stops, says so, and names the treatment that uses the incomplete rows.

"pairwise"

Each item's thresholds are estimated from the rows that observe it and each polychoric correlation from the rows that observe both items (lavaan's missing = "pairwise"); the single-factor fit, both denominators, and the assembly are otherwise unchanged. Pairwise deletion is the default treatment of missing data under WLSMV estimation in Mplus (Shi, Lee, Fairchild, & Maydeu-Olivares, 2020). Asparouhov and Muthén (2010) show it consistent when the missingness depends only on covariates in the model; a single-factor model of the items has no covariates, so here it is consistent only under MCAR, the assumption of listwise deletion. It uses more of the data than listwise deletion, not a weaker assumption: when values are missing at random (MAR), Shi et al. (2020) found the estimates of pairwise deletion severely biased, and they recommend multiple imputation. Every interval method applies, each replication resampling the rows and refitting by pairwise deletion.

"mi"

Multiple imputation, consistent when values are MAR given the items and any auxiliary variables named in aux. The items are imputed by chained equations with mice (van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011), with every other item and every auxiliary variable as a predictor and 10 iterations of the chains, and categorical omega is computed on each completed data set with the chosen denominator; the point estimate is their mean (Rubin's rule for a point estimate), and the residual polychoric correlations are averaged the same way. An auxiliary variable is a predictor in the imputation model only, never an item, so it carries information about the missing values without entering the composite. The interval is the bootstrap then impute interval of Schomaker and Heumann (2018, their Boot MI): B bootstrap samples are drawn from the incomplete rows, each is imputed imputations times, the estimate of a replication is the mean of its imputations, and the percentile interval of those means is the confidence interval. Because the imputation model is refitted on every bootstrap sample, the interval carries the sampling variability of the imputation model as well as that of the coefficient. Bartlett and Hughes (2020) found that imputing and then bootstrapping does not, in general, give valid variances when the imputation and analysis models are uncongenial, as a regression imputation model and a probit factor model are, while bootstrapping and then imputing can. Schomaker and Heumann found the coverage of Boot MI near the nominal level in their simulations, and found that pooling the estimates of every imputation of every replication into one distribution gives intervals that are too wide, which DMAR therefore never does. A completed data set of the observed data that returns no value is set aside and counted, and the point estimate averages the rest; the call stops only when fewer than half return a value. A replication computes the same statistic: the mean of those of its completed data sets that return a value, set aside when fewer than half of them return one or when its imputation fails (see When a completed data set is improper below).

When a completed data set is improper. Imputation can produce an improper single-factor solution (a standardized loading above one) in a completed data set when the observed data have none, and the example below shows how. The polychoric correlation of an item piled into its top category with one piled into its bottom category is determined by the few respondents in the cells where the two disagree, and the values missing at random given y1 and y2 are missing most often among the respondents low on them, who supply those cells. Predictive mean matching fills each missing value with the observed value of a donor whose predicted mean is close, and among the observed respondents low on y1 and y2 nearly all chose the bottom category of y3 (all but one, in the example's sample). How many imputed respondents land in the rare cells therefore varies from one completed data set to the next; where almost none do, the polychoric correlation runs toward one and the loading of y3 past it. In 100 completed data sets of the example's data, 13 were improper: 7 of the 13 in which the imputations put no respondent in the cells where y3 is above its bottom category and y1 or y2 below its top, 6 of the 58 in which they put one or two there, and none of the 29 in which they put three or more. The standard deviation of the loading of y3 over those imputations was 0.106, against 0.046 over 40 imputations under the proportional odds model. Neither that model nor more donors is a remedy: over 61 samples of the example's design the proportional odds model gave improper sets in fewer samples (5 of the 61, against 13) but estimates lower than the complete data value by 0.066 on average, and predictive mean matching with ten donors in place of five lowered the average share of improper sets only from 3% to 2%.

Categorical omega is not defined for an improper solution, so such a completed data set has no estimate, and Rubin's rules, which average an estimate from every completed data set, need one. Stopping whenever one completed data set fails, as Jia and Wu (2019) counted a replication of their simulation as failed unless all its imputations converged, makes the method fail by design: with a share \(p\) of such sets, \(M\) imputations include one with probability \(1 - (1 - p)^M\), which approaches one as von Hippel's rule asks for more imputations. The function instead sets such a completed data set aside, as it sets aside a bootstrap replication, and the point estimate averages those that returned a value, as Lim and Cheung (2022) pooled the imputations that converged and as lavaan.mi does by default for imputations that did not converge. Setting aside conditions the estimate on a property of the estimate, so the number set aside, and why, is reported in a warning and printed under the table, and the call stops when fewer than half of the completed data sets return a value, the criterion by which Lim and Cheung counted an analysis as failed. The improper sets are those with the largest loadings, so setting them aside lowers the estimate. Over the 61 samples, 13 had at least one improper completed data set among 20, with a share of 3% on average and 65% at most, and no sample's complete data or pairwise deletion fit was improper. Against refitting those sets with every loading bounded at one, setting them aside lowered the estimate by about 0.034 times the share set aside (0.0017 at 5%, a tenth of the complete data estimate's sampling standard deviation of 0.0165), and over the 13 samples the two were equally far from the complete data estimate (root mean square differences 0.0126 and 0.0122). No completed data set of the observed data is fitted after the bootstrap, so none can discard a bootstrap already run (see The number of imputations).

A bootstrap replication follows the same rule, set by set: it averages those of its \(M_b\) completed data sets that return a value and is set aside when fewer than half do, because the bootstrap distribution is that of the statistic computed as the point estimate is computed. The interval follows it too: when fewer than half of the replications return a value, none is reported, as for the other treatments (see the confidence interval methods above). Setting a replication aside whenever any one of its completed data sets returned no value would be a different statistic, and the argument above applies to it unchanged: a replication would be set aside with probability \(1 - (1 - p)^{M_b}\), so raising imputations would set more replications aside, and the completed data sets of those replications that did return a value would be discarded. In a bootstrap of the example's incomplete data under the model implied setting (B = 200, imputations = 5, seed = 1), in which a quarter of the completed data sets returned no value, that rule, applied to the first two, three, four, and five imputations of each replication, would have set aside 35.5, 45.5, 48.5, and 52.5 percent of the replications, where the rule used sets aside 12.5, 21, 14.5, and 20 percent. Under the rule used the share set aside goes to zero as \(M_b\) grows when fewer than half of the completed data sets fail, but not steadily: an odd \(M_b\) needs \((M_b + 1)/2\) of its sets to return a value, one more than the even number below it needs of one set fewer, so it sets aside more replications than either even neighbor (with a fifth of the sets failing independently, 4.0, 10.4, 2.7, and 5.8 percent at two to five imputations). Where completed data sets are set aside, an even number of imputations is the better choice, and the number the warning names is even. The warning and the imputation attribute count the completed data sets set aside within the replications kept (replicate_sets_set_aside).

The imputation model. impute = "pmm", the default, is predictive mean matching: each missing value is replaced by the observed value of the same item of a donor whose predicted mean, from a linear regression on the other variables, is close, with the regression parameters drawn anew for each imputation. It never imputes a category the item does not show, though a category rare among the observed values is rarely drawn. impute = "polr" is the proportional odds model, with every other item entering as a factor (a binary item is imputed by logistic regression, the same model for two categories). mice draws its categories at the model's point estimates, without drawing the model's parameters, and Jia and Wu (2019), pooling its imputations in the usual way, found acceptable loading estimates but confidence intervals that were too narrow under missingness at random; under bootstrap then impute the refit on every bootstrap sample supplies the variability of the imputation model instead. The default rests on a Monte Carlo simulation run for this function: 10 items, one factor with loadings from .50 to .80, \(n = 300\), and items 6 to 10 missing at random given the mean of items 1 to 5, about 21% of the values in all. Against the complete data estimate of the same sample, the mean categorical omega was off by -0.0035 with five categories (100 replications) and by +0.0015 with three skewed categories (60 replications) under predictive mean matching; by -0.019 and +0.035 under the proportional odds model; by -0.028 and -0.047 under pairwise deletion; and by -0.105 with five categories under listwise deletion, which with three categories failed in 55 of the 60 samples. A replication under predictive mean matching was also about ten times faster (see Run time below). The evidence is one factor structure and one missing data mechanism, so with very rare categories or another mechanism the comparison could differ.

Every incomplete item is imputed. By default mice stops imputing a variable whose correlation with another, computed from the rows that observe both, reaches .999 in absolute value; two items observed together on only two or three rows, as in a planned missing design with a small overlap, reach it by arithmetic, and the item left with its missing values would then be fitted by listwise deletion inside each completed data set. That check is therefore turned off, an item with a single observed value is refused before anything is imputed, and an item mice still does not impute stops the call with its name.

The same check also set aside an auxiliary variable that duplicates another (a score and its rescaling, age in years and in months). Without it both reach every item's regression, and when the predictors carry a second exact dependency (a second such pair, or an auxiliary variable computed from complete items) mice 3.19.0 removes only one of them and falls back to a ridge penalty, after which its imputations are unstable: on the five-item example of the tests, an auxiliary variable computed from the first three items and its rescaling gave 0.768 with a between-imputation standard deviation of 0.062, against 0.800 and 0.008 without them. So the auxiliary variables are screened before anything is imputed: one whose multiple correlation with the columns observed on every row that observes it (the items and the auxiliary variables kept before it) reaches .999, mice's own threshold for a pair, is a linear function of predictors already in the model, carries no information about the missing values, and is left out, with a message naming it; the items are not screened, so a planned missing design is still imputed in full. When mice still applies its ridge penalty, which it does when the predictors of an item are (nearly) linearly dependent, the warning says how often, and the imputation attribute counts it (ridge).

The items are imputed as plain integer codes, whatever their class: a column read with haven, which carries value labels, and a factor whose labels are whole numbers are both accepted (see the data argument), and the imputation model is the one for the codes. SPSS user-defined missing values, which haven::read_sav(user_na = TRUE) keeps as values of a haven_labelled_spss column, are missing under every treatment, as SPSS and haven's is.na() treat them.

The number of imputations. Each bootstrap replication is imputed imputations times (\(M_b\), 20 by default). The variance of a replicate mean is the sampling variance of the coefficient plus the imputation variance divided by \(M_b\), so imputation noise widens the percentile interval by about \(\sqrt{1 + \gamma / M_b}\), where \(\gamma\) is the fraction of missing information: by 1.5% at \(\gamma = .15\) and by 4.9% at \(\gamma = .50\) with five imputations. The function estimates \(\gamma\) from the replications themselves, by the one-way analysis of variance of the replicate by imputation estimates (the variance between replications net of the imputation variance within them, which is the sampling variance with infinitely many imputations, against the imputation variance), reports the widening, and warns when it exceeds 5%, naming the value of imputations that would bring it under; when no interval is reported (fewer than half of the replications returned a value) neither the warning nor the printed line gives a widening, and the printed fraction of missing information is marked as that of the replications that returned one. A replication that sets some of its completed data sets aside averages \(n_b < M_b\) of them, and the analysis of variance is then the unbalanced one (Searle, Casella, & McCulloch, 1992, Sec. 3.6), whose interval for the ratio of the variances is approximate; the widening is \(\sqrt{1 + \gamma \, \overline{1/n_b}}\), the mean taken over the replications, and the value of imputations named allows for the share of completed data sets set aside and is even when any were, whether in the replications kept or in those set aside for them, but not when only the imputation itself failed (see When a completed data set is improper). Schomaker and Heumann (2018) found that Boot MI can do well with fewer than five imputations per replication and covers too often with one. The point estimate averages \(M_0\) imputations of the observed data: at least 20 and at least imputations, and more when von Hippel's (2020, Eq. 1) quadratic rule, \(M = 1 + \frac{1}{2}(\gamma / \mathrm{CV})^2\) with \(\mathrm{CV} = .05\), asks for more at the upper limit of a 95% confidence interval for \(\gamma\), as his two stage procedure uses it (here the limit for the ratio of variance components in the same analysis of variance). His target is the replicability of a standard error from Rubin's rules, which bootstrap then impute does not use; the rule is borrowed to keep the point estimate from changing much if the data were imputed again, with the bootstrap as the pilot. Since the rule asks for at most 201 imputations (at \(\gamma = 1\)), a call with a bootstrap makes that many imputations of the observed data, and fits and checks each, before the bootstrap runs, and the point estimate then uses the first \(M_0\) of them, the number fixed by the rule and the floor and never by their estimates. Nothing found in a completed data set of the observed data can then discard a finished bootstrap; the imputations the rule does not use cost at most 181 imputations and fits, less than 1% of the 20000 of the default bootstrap. The estimate of \(\gamma\) is imprecise when B is small, and under impute = "polr", whose imputations ignore the uncertainty of the imputation model's parameters, it is too low. Without a bootstrap the point estimate averages max(imputations, 20) imputations, which keeps Rubin's relative efficiency, \((1 + \gamma / M)^{-1}\), at .976 or above for \(\gamma\) up to .5. The se row is the standard error of the point estimate, \(\sqrt{s^2_{boot} + s^2_{imp} / M_0}\), with \(s^2_{boot}\) the sampling variance and \(s^2_{imp}\) the imputation variance from the same analysis of variance, so it counts the noise of the point estimate's own imputations. The analysis of variance is a construction for this function, not a published procedure for omega.

Run time under multiple imputation. A replication imputes its resample imputations times and refits the factor model on each completed data set, so the run time grows with B times imputations. With 10 items, five categories, and 300 cases, a replication with five imputations took about half a second under predictive mean matching and about five seconds under the proportional odds model, so the default B = 1000 runs for about eight minutes and well over an hour, respectively, on one core with five imputations. The default of 20 imputations per replication does about four times that imputation and fitting work. This larger default reduces imputation noise; it has not been separately calibrated for interval coverage. The default B is 1000 under missing = "mi" rather than the 10000 of the other two treatments (a percentile interval reads its limits from less extreme quantiles than BCa), and why BCa, whose jackknife would add imputations imputations per case, is refused. ncpus spreads the replications over processes; every resample, and a seed for each replication's imputations, is drawn before any replication runs, so a given seed returns the same result whatever ncpus is.

Comparison with other packages. The psych package's omega fits a Schmid-Leiman hierarchical factor model to Pearson correlations or, with poly = TRUE, to polychoric correlations, and does not implement categorical omega in the sense of Green and Yang (2009), which reliability_omega_categorical computes for ordered-categorical items; polychoric provides polychoric correlation estimation as a separate tool.

Examples

set.seed(113)
# The mixed-skew design of Green and Yang (2009, Table 1): four items
# loading 0.8 on one factor, each cut into five categories, two piled
# into the top category and two into the bottom. Their population
# categorical omega for this design is 0.716.
N <- 1000
p_top <- c(.011, .027, .047, .118, .797)
cut_top <- c(-Inf, qnorm(cumsum(p_top)[-5]), Inf)
cut_bottom <- c(-Inf, qnorm(cumsum(rev(p_top))[-5]), Inf)
latent <- outer(rnorm(N), rep(0.8, 4)) +
          matrix(rnorm(N * 4, sd = 0.6), N, 4)
items <- cbind(y1 = cut(latent[, 1], cut_top, labels = FALSE),
               y2 = cut(latent[, 2], cut_top, labels = FALSE),
               y3 = cut(latent[, 3], cut_bottom, labels = FALSE),
               y4 = cut(latent[, 4], cut_bottom, labels = FALSE))

# Categorical omega as Green and Yang defined it: the total variance
# of the summed categories comes from the correlations the fitted
# single-factor model reproduces.
reliability_omega_categorical(data = items, denominator = "model_implied")
#> Categorical omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "bca" (the recommended method) or "percentile"; B = 10000 replications is the default when you do.
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.714
#>  se         <NA> 
#>  ci_lower   <NA> 
#>  ci_upper   <NA> 
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          1000 
#>  N_complete 1000 
#>  n_items    4    
#> 
#> Denominator: variance of the summed categories from the model implied polychoric correlations (Green & Yang, 2009)
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: 0.028 (y1 with y4)

# The default, categorical omega as Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016)
# computed and recommended it: the total variance comes from the
# unrestricted polychoric correlations. The single factor holds in
# this design, so the two agree to within about 0.01; they part ways
# as the model misfits.
reliability_omega_categorical(data = items)
#> Categorical omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "bca" (the recommended method) or "percentile"; B = 10000 replications is the default when you do.
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.720
#>  se         <NA> 
#>  ci_lower   <NA> 
#>  ci_upper   <NA> 
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          1000 
#>  N_complete 1000 
#>  n_items    4    
#> 
#> Denominator: variance of the summed categories from the unrestricted polychoric correlations (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016)
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: 0.028 (y1 with y4)

# The same sum score with the items treated as continuous. Robust
# omega falls far below 0.716 here, because items whose categories
# pile up at opposite ends relate to the factor far from linearly,
# which is the case Green and Yang designed their coefficient for.
reliability_omega(data = items)
#> Robust omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "percentile" (or "bca"); B = 10000 replications is the default when you do.
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.549
#>  se         <NA> 
#>  ci_lower   <NA> 
#>  ci_upper   <NA> 
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          1000 
#>  N_complete 1000 
#>  n_items    4    
#> 
#> Denominator: observed composite variance (robust omega)
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: 0.283 (y3 with y4)

# The same items with values missing at random: respondents low on y1
# and y2 leave y3 and y4 unanswered more often. Listwise deletion, the
# default, keeps only the complete rows, and here that leaves too
# little: the few respondents who determine the correlation of a
# top-piled item with a bottom-piled one (one to five of the 1000 for
# each pair) stand low on y1 and y2, the complete rows keep none of
# them for y2 with y3 or for y1 with y4, and the correlations left do
# not identify the loadings, so a call with the default stops and says
# so (see Details).
z <- as.numeric(scale(items[, "y1"] + items[, "y2"]))
items_mar <- items
items_mar[runif(N) < plogis(-1.5 - 1.2 * z), "y3"] <- NA
items_mar[runif(N) < plogis(-1.5 - 1.2 * z), "y4"] <- NA

# Pairwise deletion estimates each polychoric correlation from the rows
# that observe both items, so every row contributes. It still assumes
# values missing completely at random, as listwise deletion does.
# Multiple imputation, which assumes only that they are missing at
# random, takes longer than an example here can (see Details).
reliability_omega_categorical(data = items_mar,
                              denominator = "model_implied",
                              missing = "pairwise")
#> The data do not determine the polychoric correlation of y2 and y3 (the bivariate table has empty cells). The model implied denominator does not need it, and the correlations the data do determine identify the single-factor loadings; its residual correlation is reported as NA.
#> Categorical omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "bca" (the recommended method) or "percentile"; B = 10000 replications is the default when you do.
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.691
#>  se         <NA> 
#>  ci_lower   <NA> 
#>  ci_upper   <NA> 
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          1000 
#>  N_complete 686  
#>  n_items    4    
#> 
#> Denominator: variance of the summed categories from the model implied polychoric correlations (Green & Yang, 2009)
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: 0.029 (y2 with y4)
#> 
#> Missing data: pairwise deletion, consistent only when values are missing completely at random, as listwise deletion is (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010); it uses more of the data, not a weaker assumption, and missing = "mi" is the remedy when values are missing at random
